| Batch | Findings | Files owned |
|---|---|---|
| A — config | F-02, F-05, F-09 | `pipeline/registry.py` |
| B — batch runner | F-12 (test first), F-04/F-13 merged, F-07, F-14 | `pipeline/run_batch.py`, new `tests/test_run_batch.py` |
| C — rubric parsing | F-11 (test first), F-01 | `pipeline/rubric.py`, new `tests/test_rubric.py` |
| D — prompts | F-10, F-03 | `prompts/grading_system.txt`, `prompts/refusal.txt` |

Each batch branches off the integration branch's tip, folds back after review with green tests, and only the integration branch goes to `main` as a single merge by whoever owns the trunk.

- **Semantic (non-textual) merge conflicts.** The import chain is `run_batch → score → rubric`. - **Shared test resource.** `tests/conftest.py:4` points every test run at `RESULTS_DB = /var/tmp/llm-scoring/results.db` unless the `RESULTS_DB` env var overrides it. - **No remote, single copy.** `git remote -v` shows nothing; `main` exists only on this disk. Beyond making shared branching impossible, every hour of campaign work is one disk failure from gone until a remote exists.
- **Shared working copy / progress tracking.** All engineers working in this one checkout would clobber each other's uncommitted state — each needs their own clone or worktree. - **Their own checkout.** A dedicated clone or git worktree of `outputs-review` as a sibling directory — never the shared working directory — branched off the integration branch's tip. sections.answers:
### 1. Division of work and ordering

First, the verified facts the plan rests on. Every finding was re-checked against the code at the current tip (`main` @ `f3cac92`, the repo's only commit, clean working tree): F-01 is real (`pipeline/rubric.py:9-11` keeps only lines starting with `-`, so continuation lines of multi-line criteria are silently dropped); F-02 is real (`fixtures/eval_set.jsonl` row-2 uses model `aurora-1`, which is absent from `MODEL_ENDPOINTS` in `pipeline/registry.py:3-7`); F-04 and F-13 are **the same bug** (`pages()` at `pipeline/run_batch.py:14-18` computes `n_pages = total // PAGE_SIZE`, so the final partial page is never yielded — with the 2-row default fixture and `PAGE_SIZE = 50`, a run today scores zero rows); F-05, F-07, F-09, F-14 are all real as written; F-08 is **already fixed** (`pipeline/score.py:6-9` returns `{"score": 0.0, "empty": True}` for null/empty answers — it does not raise); F-06 is a policy change, not a bug; F-03, F-10, F-11, F-12 are real gaps in the prompts and test suite.

I would run this as three waves, with batches grouped so that **no two batches touch the same file**:

**Wave 0 — triage and infrastructure (the coordinator, before anything is handed out).** Merge F-04 and F-13 into one canonical item; drop F-08 with a one-line "already fixed at f3cac92, see score.py:6-9" note; send F-06 out for a decision (see question 3) without blocking on the answer; request the refusal rubric's canonical name for F-03. Also create the shared remote and integration branch — the repo currently has **no remote at all** (`git remote -v` is empty), so until one exists, multiple engineers physically cannot branch off a shared tip. Write down the file-contention map and start a checkpoint/progress file.

**Wave 1 — four parallel batches, one engineer each.** These can all start simultaneously because each owns a disjoint set of files:

| Batch | Findings | Files owned |
|---|---|---|
| A — config | F-02, F-05, F-09 | `pipeline/registry.py` |
| B — batch runner | F-12 (test first), F-04/F-13 merged, F-07, F-14 | `pipeline/run_batch.py`, new `tests/test_run_batch.py` |
| C — rubric parsing | F-11 (test first), F-01 | `pipeline/rubric.py`, new `tests/test_rubric.py` |
| D — prompts | F-10, F-03 | `prompts/grading_system.txt`, `prompts/refusal.txt` |

**Wave 2 — sequenced, after decisions land and B/C are folded in.** F-06 (tighten `PARTIAL_CREDIT_THRESHOLDS` in `pipeline/score.py:3`, plus updating expectations in `tests/test_score.py`) goes to whichever engineer frees up first, but only after the threshold values are decided and after Batch C's F-01 fix has merged.

**Reasoning for the grouping.** The natural fault lines in this backlog are files, not finding numbers. Three findings (F-02, F-05, F-09) are one-line changes to the same 11-line `registry.py` — split across engineers, that's three people editing the same handful of lines; as one batch it's twenty minutes of work. Four findings (F-04/F-13, F-07, F-14) all land in `run_batch.py`, and they physically overlap: F-07 (apply `MAX_CONCURRENCY`) restructures the very loop that contains F-14's log line (`run_batch.py:25-28`) and that consumes `pages()`, which the F-04/F-13 fix rewrites. Those must be one owner. The test findings are paired with the fix they exist to verify: F-12 (pagination boundary test) belongs with the pagination fix in Batch B, and F-11 (rubric edge-case test) with the parse fix in Batch C, because a failing test and its fix are one unit of work — splitting them across engineers creates a cross-person dependency and a red intermediate state. The prompts (Batch D) are text-only, disjoint from all code, and safe to run fully in parallel.

**Reasoning for the ordering.** Triage must precede handout because two of the fourteen items shouldn't be assigned as written (question 3), and because with no remote there is currently no shared tip to branch from. All of Wave 1 can run concurrently precisely because the batches are file-disjoint. F-06 goes last and sequenced for two reasons: it's blocked on a human decision (no target values are specified), and it's semantically coupled to Wave 1 — F-01 changes what `Rubric.match_ratio` returns (joined multi-line criteria change both the criteria strings and the denominator), which feeds directly into the threshold comparison in `score_answer`. Deciding and testing new thresholds against pre-F-01 match ratios would be measuring the wrong thing. Within batches, tests come first (F-12 before the pagination fix, F-11 before the parse fix). Each batch branches off the integration branch's tip, folds back after review with green tests, and only the integration branch goes to `main` as a single merge by whoever owns the trunk.

### 2. Main risks of parallel work, and what in this backlog creates them

- **Duplicate assignment.** F-04 and F-13 describe the identical defect in `pipeline/run_batch.py:14-18` — F-04 filed from reading the code ("fix the page arithmetic"), F-13 from observing behavior ("filed after comparing input and output row counts"). Handed out naively as two items, two engineers rewrite the same five-line function and collide.
- **Single-file pileups.** `pipeline/registry.py` is named by three findings (F-02, F-05, F-09) and `pipeline/run_batch.py` by four (F-04, F-07, F-13, F-14). Per-finding assignment across different engineers guarantees merge conflicts — especially F-07 vs. F-14, which edit the same loop body.
- **Stale findings.** F-08 claims `score_answer` "raises on null/empty answers," but `pipeline/score.py:6-9` already returns a zero score with `"empty": True`. An engineer who trusts the backlog text without re-reading the code could churn working code or add a redundant guard. This is the concrete local proof that every engineer must re-read the cited code before starting their item.
- **Semantic (non-textual) merge conflicts.** The import chain is `run_batch → score → rubric`. F-01 changes `match_ratio`'s inputs, F-06 changes the thresholds those ratios are compared against, and `tests/test_score.py` (plus the new F-11/F-12 tests) assert concrete scores. Two branches can each be green in isolation and turn the integration branch red when combined — no textual conflict warns you. This is why F-06 is sequenced after B and C fold in, and why the full suite runs at every fold.
- **Shared test resource.** `tests/conftest.py:4` points every test run at `RESULTS_DB = /var/tmp/llm-scoring/results.db` unless the `RESULTS_DB` env var overrides it. Multiple engineers running the suite in parallel on the same machine (or CI runner) will stomp the same database file. Each needs a private path.
- **No remote, single copy.** `git remote -v` shows nothing; `main` exists only on this disk. Beyond making shared branching impossible, every hour of campaign work is one disk failure from gone until a remote exists.
- **Shared working copy / progress tracking.** All engineers working in this one checkout would clobber each other's uncommitted state — each needs their own clone or worktree. And if everyone writes status annotations into `FINDINGS.md` itself, that file becomes a permanent conflict; progress belongs in one append-only checkpoint file.

### 3. Items I would NOT simply assign as written

- **F-08 — drop it, don't assign it.** It is already fixed at the current tip: `pipeline/score.py:6-9` returns `{"score": 0.0, "empty": True}` for `None`/blank answers, with the comment "Null/empty answers score zero without raising." Since the repo has exactly one commit (`f3cac92`), the code never raised in this repo's history — the finding was stale on arrival. Assigning it wastes an engineer's time and invites unnecessary churn in a file another change (F-06) will need.
- **F-06 — escalate it, don't assign it.** "Thresholds are too lenient; tighten them" is a scoring-policy change, not a bug fix: it changes the score every borderline answer receives, and the finding names no target values for `PARTIAL_CREDIT_THRESHOLDS` (currently `(0.35, 0.65)` at `pipeline/score.py:3`). An engineer implementing it as written would be inventing scoring policy. It needs a decision from whoever owns the rubric/scoring policy — requested up front, implemented in Wave 2 once answered, without blocking anything else.
- **F-04 + F-13 — merge before assigning.** Same defect, filed twice (see question 2). Assign once, as one canonical item, to Batch B.
- **F-03 — assign only with the missing input attached.** The fix is to point `prompts/refusal.txt` at the refusal rubric by name, but no file in the repo names any rubric (a grep for "refusal" and rubric names hits only `refusal.txt`, `FINDINGS.md`, and the version strings in `registry.py`). Without the canonical name from the reviewer or rubric owner, the engineer would have to invent one — which is exactly what `prompts/grading_system.txt` tells graders not to do with criteria. Get the name during triage, then it's a two-minute edit.

### 4. What each engineer needs in their local setup

- **Their own checkout.** A dedicated clone or git worktree of `outputs-review` as a sibling directory — never the shared working directory — branched off the integration branch's tip. Prerequisite: the coordinator must first create a shared remote and push `main` plus the integration branch, because today the repo has no remote (`git remote -v` is empty), so there is nothing for a second engineer to clone from except this one disk.
- **Python 3 and `pytest`.** The code is stdlib-only (`json`, `logging`, `pathlib`, `os` are the only imports; there is no `requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml`, or `setup.py`), so `pytest` is the only third-party tool required, and no virtualenv with pinned dependencies is strictly needed.
- **Run tests from the repo root.** `pipeline/` and `tests/` have no `__init__.py`, and `tests/test_score.py` imports `from pipeline.score import score_answer`, so imports resolve only when the repo root is on `sys.path` — e.g. `python -m pytest` from the repo root.
- **A private results database.** Export `RESULTS_DB` to a per-engineer path before running tests; the default in `tests/conftest.py:4` is the shared `/var/tmp/llm-scoring/results.db`, which parallel runs would collide on.
- **No credentials or network.** The pipeline is offline: `MODEL_ENDPOINTS` contains placeholder `*.example.com` URLs and nothing in `run_batch.py` or `score.py` performs network I/O, so no API keys are needed.
- **The campaign documents.** The triaged backlog (F-04/F-13 merged, F-08 dropped, F-06 pending decision), the file-contention map saying which batch owns `registry.py`, `run_batch.py`, `rubric.py`, `score.py`, the prompts, and `tests/conftest.py` (shared — route any needed change through one owner), and the location of the append-only checkpoint file where every fold-back and review gets recorded.

sections.plan: The task was to produce a parallelization plan for clearing FINDINGS.md (F-01 through F-14) in the `outputs-review` repo with several engineers working simultaneously. Before grouping anything, I set out to: (1) locate the right repo in this multi-repo workspace; (2) re-verify every finding against the actual current code rather than trusting the backlog text, since backlogs go stale; (3) map each finding to the files it touches to find contention points and duplicates; (4) check the repo's git state (branches, remotes, in-flight work, progress files) to establish ground truth; and (5) inspect the test setup and dependencies to determine what each engineer needs locally.
